title: Hakuin's Song of Zazen
speaker: Koshin Chris Cain
summary: Koshin Chris Cain takes up Hakuin's Song of Zazen, reading it in full after a sketch of Hakuin's life. Koshin tells of the eleven-year-old terrified by a preacher's eight hot hells, who turns to Tenjin and Kannon for protection, later becomes a monk, suffers Zen sickness, and wakes at 42 while reading the Lotus Sutra. Koshin then works through the song's images of ice and water, the young fish who asks "What is water?", and the line "Is anything missing now?" Questions close the evening, covering Hakuin's death, his love of sweets and tobacco, and the nights he sat bound in a mattress.

Nomon, thank you so much for having me.
We've talked about this for a while, and I'm happy to be here.
Nomon and I are in a group, maybe many of you know already, but maybe some of you don't know.
We're in a group of peers, teachers, and we meet together every couple of months.
We meet together this Sunday.
And we talk about what it is to be a teacher in the West.
You know, it's two Rinzai and two Soto and somebody who's in between.
And we just, it's so evident that we're all trying to figure this out, how to do this practice and help people in this brand new context for Buddhism.
I'm bringing you something today from the Rinzai tradition.
I asked Nomon, should I say, I've got some great things to say about Dogen.
He said, no, why don't you just stay in your lane.
So I'm bringing Hakuen to you today.
Has anybody read Hakuen here?
Well, Hakuen's a, you know, he's an interesting read.
He's kind of exciting.
I'm not sure I would have liked him if I had known him or what he'd be like as a teacher.
He's very passionate and strong and sometimes braggadocious and sometimes tender.
So I'm gonna talk about Hakuen's Song of Zazen tonight.
It's a very nice thing.
We chant it sometimes at our place.
And so I'll read it in just a moment.
And then I'll say something about it.
But before that, I'll tell you something about Hakuen.
He was born in 1686 and died, you know, 80 years later.
So just before the Revolutionary War in this country.
And when he died, he was the most respected teacher in Japan, a Zen teacher in Japan.
And I, you know, how do you gauge these things?
But sometimes they say in books, he was probably the most influential Zen master of the last 500 years.
I kind of don't doubt it.
I mean, I would think that as a Rinzai person, but really he's one of the luminaries in the Zen world.
And he revitalized a Rinzai practice, which had gotten kind of calcified and stagnant and real interested in the arts.
You know, we did, we came up with the tea ceremony and we then we got real good at it.
And some other things like that too.
He was a great, I mean, I wish I had brought some pictures of his, not just the calligraphy, but the artwork of his too, because it's not fine, but it's full of life and exciting.
I love it.
So anyway, Hakuin, he really walked to the beat of his own drum.
And as for instance, he wrote his own autobiography, which I don't know had it ever been done.
Anyway, very rare in those days for anything like that to happen.
You die and then your students write about you.
But he wrote his own, which gives us a lot of detail actually about his life.
It's quite a nice resource, of course, from his perspective.
But in that autobiography, it's called Wild Ivy.
It's evident that as a child, he ran hot.
He got very excited about certain things and worried.
In his autobiography, he recounts the story when he was 11 years old.
He heard this traveling preacher from the Nichiren sect.
His mother was Nichiren.
And the Nichiren sect, especially in those days, they could be pretty powerful.
And so this traveling preacher was talking about the eight hot hells and what would happen in each one of those hells when he died.
He was 11 years old.
I don't know if anybody grew up fundamentalist.
Yeah, there you go.
So you know all about the eight hot hells.
Yeah.
And what an effect, right?
What an emotional effect it can have on somebody.
I didn't.
I had a Presbyterian.
My Presbyterian used to call us God's frozen people.
But this was not frozen.
This is hot.
And so he was taking a bath that night after that.
And in Japan, if anybody's been, they like their baths hot.
So this was a hot bath.
And he freaked out.
He had a complete meltdown.
He couldn't get in the bath.
And you know, worried about the hot hells and what's going to happen.
And how can I be protected?
And his mother just embraced him.
He had a very tender, very, very loving mother who was quick to help other people.
And she said, Just calm down.
I'll tell you the secret of how to escape the hot hells tomorrow.
Just get some sleep.
That's very smart.
I had kids my own.
I know it's much better to talk about things in the morning if you can get in there.
So then the next day she said, Okay, what you have to do is you have to worship at the Buddhist shrine to Tenjin, a certain Buddhist deity.
I think it was a deity.
So he did chanting practice to Tenjin.
And then not long afterwards, he was playing with a bow and arrow and accidentally shot his brother's poster of some samurai.
Not a poster, a piece of art, of course, but you know, you can do the head up on his wall.
Some samurai, his favorite samurai shot right through the eye.
And his brother wasn't around.
His parents were going to kill him.
You know, he was sure.
And so he prayed to Tenjin, Please don't let them know while they came home.
And it became evident what had happened.
And his mother, of course, was was doesn't mention his father, but his mother was disappointed, but not scolding.
But for Hakuen, he thought if Tenjin can't save me from this little thing, how's he going to save me from hell?
So he gave up on Tenjin and found somebody else to ask.
And that person said, You should try Quan Yin.
And so we tried Quan Yin and that didn't calm him enough.
So finally, he saw this priest that that was, you know, you have to wonder like what was going on in those days.
I wish I could be a fly on the wall sometimes.
But this traveling priest, Buddhist priest who who could put like a red hot plowshare on his arms and and bear the pain and then put a red hot cauldron over his head.
And he realized, OK, that's what I need to do, because that guy hasn't figured out how to get, you know, live with pain and with with heat, the heat of hell.
So he really did become a Buddhist monk and checked himself in.
He was pretty critical in his early days.
I think he was about 14 when he went into the monastery.
He was critical in those days.
He traveled around a lot.
He was critical of the study, all the study that they were doing and the kind of arts practice they were doing.
He wanted to be more serious.
I think the turning point for him, and he wasn't sure he went through bouts of real, should I be a Buddhist monk?
What am I doing?
He got word at a certain monastery that his mother had died and had sent him into a deep depression.
And there's this story that's kind of well known in Rinzai circles where he just decides, OK, I'm going to reach out my hand and just pick a book.
And that's for inspiration, which doesn't matter whether it's Confucian or Taoist or Buddhist.
So he picks one out and he gets this story about this monk who's, I can't remember, I didn't write his name down, who was a disciple of the disciple of Rinzai.
And he sits all night in the cold.
And when he gets tired, freezing weather, and when he gets tired, he stabs himself with an awl.
I was told that story when I was a monk, you know, like early on.
So then he realized, that's what I've got to do.
I've got to just by myself turn toward this practice.
My interpretation of that is that he was wanting to be sheltered from the hot hells.
He was wanting to be sheltered from life.

So he went forward and at 24, he had his first great awakening when he heard the sound of the bell.
He was quite sure that this was the greatest awakening of the last 300 years.
That's the way he ran.
But he was also honest enough to notice after a few months it wore off.
And he admitted that as much, he admitted as much, that he couldn't bring it into life.
He couldn't really integrate it into his life.
And throughout, when I read Hakuen, not just his biography, but letters of his too, I'm struck by his honesty.
He, you know, again, he has this kind of braggadocious side, but he also is, I think, at critical times honest with himself.
So he practiced more day and night and I won't go into all the details, but one famous chapter of his life that I'll just mention is he got Zen sickness.
Anybody heard of the Zen sickness story?
Yeah.
And he really had a breakdown, he had a physical and mental breakdown, and went to try to find somebody to help him with it within the tradition.
And he couldn't get the help he needed.
And so he went out to an old Taoist hermit out in the woods.
That's also a little signal, I think.
He didn't mind where he went to find this wisdom.
And that Taoist hermit really cured him.
I think it's called the hot butter method.
And you can read about that.
So then many other things happened.
His father died.
He went back to this little temple and at 40 and then there was just ramshackle in the countryside outside what is now Tokyo.
And he had his great awakening at 42.
At 42 his great awakening was while reading the Lotus Sutra, which he had in his younger days hated.
He'd think it was just a collection of stories about cause and effect.
A bunch of stories about cause and effect.
And of course it was his mother's dearest sutra for the Nichiren sect.
He was reading the Lotus Sutra and he got his great enlightenment while reading that.
So he kind of came full circle.
And what he realized right after his enlightenment was that bodhi mind means helping others.
That was his great realization.
When he practiced, when he taught, he stressed the importance of an active practice, honest and curious.
And of course one that incorporates it into our lives.
He was very critical of the do nothing Zen crowd.
I don't actually think that was the Soto people.
I don't think so.
But I think it was, in fact, he visited all three types and he just didn't like that type that rested in there.
I suppose in their realization.
He was famous also for post Satori training.
You may have a realization, but you have to train afterwards.
That was really not talked about in the same way as he talked about it.
He always stayed.
He never moved from that place.
They wanted him to go to Myoshinji.
He became very famous and they wanted him to go to Myoshinji and become the abbot or something there and he wouldn't.
So he just stayed there and people poured in after many years, you know, 10 or 15 years he was practicing there.
And then people heard about him and they poured in from all over monks.
This is the first time that had ever happened, that a kind of religious community sprung up.
I mean hundreds of people.
They were living out of the countryside.
They were taking over old buildings and they got a whole scene together, a whole practicing scene.
He made up koans.
Instead of people giving people moo, you know, moo.
Everybody has moo first.
He gave people first the sound of one hand clapping, his own koan.
So that's guts.
And he didn't, when he talked to other people, he didn't mind using references from Taoism, from Confucianism, as well as from Buddhism and other Japanese traditions.
So this is his song.
Already gone for so long.
I'm going to make it short, this other part.
Hakuen song of Zazen.
All beings by nature are Buddha, as ice by nature is water.
Apart from water there is no ice, apart from beans no Buddha.
How sad that people ignore the near and search for the truth afar.
Like someone in the midst of water, crying out in thirst.
Like a child of a wealthy home wandering among the poor.
Lost on dark paths of ignorance, we wander through the six worlds from dark path to dark path.
When shall we be freed from birth and death?
Oh, the Zazen of the Mahayana.
To this the highest praise.
Devotion, repentance, training, the many paramitas all have their source in Zazen.
Those who try Zazen even once wipe away beginningless crimes.
Where are all the dark paths then?
The pure land itself is near.
Those who hear this truth even once and listen with a grateful heart,
treasuring it, revering it, gain blessings without end.
Much more those who turn about and bear witness to self-nature, self-nature that is no nature, go far beyond mere doctrine.
Here effect and cause are the same.
The way is neither two nor three.
With form that is no form, going and coming we are never astray.
With thought that is no thought, singing and dancing are the voice of the law.
Boundless and free is the sky of Samadhi, bright the full moon of wisdom.
Truly is anything missing now?
Nirvana is right here before our eyes.
This very place is the lotus land, this very body the Buddha.
I love that song.
He did it for common people.
It wasn't so much for monks.
It begins, all beings by nature are Buddha, as ice by nature is water.
A foundational part of our practice is to get a feeling.
For Buddhism says is a fact that we are not just ourselves.
No, we're not just Kate and no more than Gosha and John.
We're also, though we may not always be conscious of it, Buddha.
We have this other nature that is subtle and happy and luminous.
An aspect that we all share that the way I feel is waiting kind of to be discovered.
That's covered over, waiting to become manifest.
When we are manifesting that aspect, things are fine.
I think of Hakuen's mother and her love for him.
No matter what, she was there for him, no matter what he was feeling.
I'm sure no matter what crazy profession he chose or what prison he ended up in, she would embrace him.
The Buddha called the route to this, to realizing this Buddha nature, present moment awareness.
This present moment awareness, of course, is with us always; it's always available to us.
This means that we have to drop our regular everyday way of approaching the world and see things that we don't normally see.
There's a lot of water imagery in this Song of Zazen, which also reminds me of this story of two young fish swimming along and they meet an older fish.
The older fish says, "Hey boys, how's the water?" and then swims along.
And then the one young fish says to the other, "What the hell is water?"
That's from a very famous David Foster Wallace talk as a commencement address that I really appreciate.
Our practice is to become aware of this water that we float in, this world that we so often ignore.
Hakuin starts with a block of ice and says that we are water.
He chooses that metaphor intentionally, I'm sure, because ice doesn't know it's water most of the time; it just always has been ice.
But with someone tells it's water, our practice to further confuse this water metaphor really is to get a feeling for that water aspect.
I think water is fluid; it moves easily, it meets whatever comes, whether it's something we like or something we don't like, whether it's joy or sadness.
I think this practice does allow us to melt a little bit and become less fixed in our views and in our identity.
So we are both solid and flowing at the same time, according to Hakuin.
He says, "Apart from water, there is no ice; apart from beings, no Buddha."
Apart from water, there is no ice.
I'm just going to unpack this, then I'm going to go very quickly.
According to the tradition, there is no ice that is not water.
That's another way to put that.
According to tradition, we all have this water aspect.
We all have this Buddha nature.
We all have different selves; a bird has a bird self, a cat has a cat self.
But we share this Buddha nature.
When we're at a restful state, we have the same zero.
Then he says, "Apart from beings, there is no Buddha."
And that means, I think, that there is no Buddha nature floating around out there.
There is no Buddha looking over everything.
It doesn't exist except as an aspect of ourselves.
I think that's something that is important to remember.
And I think it's also a foundational part of Zen.
There's no mystical force out there; it's just an aspect of you and me.
Then he goes on to say that it's always with us, just like water, even though we're thirsty.
And that it's the very bedrock of our practice.
He's skipping on much closer to the end and gets to the promise of practice.

That if you hear this, and if you not only hear it once but manifest it, that bear witness to the self-nature that is no nature, he says, "With form that is no form, going and coming, we are never astray.
We are at home with both form and no form.
We're at home with ice, and we're at home with water.
Going and coming, we're never astray."
The word Tathagata is kind of a play I've heard.
It can either mean one who is thus come or one who is thus gone, depending on how it's pronounced.

I think that this practice really does help us as we get to know it: go and come freely between self and no self, between the world of Buddha and the world of humans, between life and death, expanding and contracting.
And that is real freedom.
We tend to think, I think, of freedom as freedom of choice in our living world.
But I think real freedom is the freedom to die and to live.
What we tend to think of freedom is, I think, is a limited view.
It's a little bit like me saying to my kids, "Well, tonight, would you like peas or carrots?"
See, there's a choice; there's freedom there, but it's limited.
I hope they don't think about the fact that they could have ice cream.
So the hope for my life, really, is that as I age in this practice, that there become within me friendlier relations—friendlier relations between my life aspect and my death aspect.
That I can both hold on and let go.
Steaming onto the end here, with thought that is no thought, "Singing and dancing are the voice of the law."
I think when we know both sides, when we really get an easy feeling between going back and forth, then the law doesn't just come from the Buddha; it comes from everything.
"Boundless and free is the sky of samadhi, bright the full moon of wisdom."
Samadhi in this is this flowing aspect, boundless and free.
Boundless and free, freely moving.
And I do feel that our practice is this practice that is of sitting still, really, is so that we can move.
So that we can move more ably, so that we can walk into a room with a difficult situation in it and be calm and approach it with something other than reactivity.
That we can walk through that, that we can go into a church and feel and go along with what's happening.
That we can make it through a Thanksgiving dinner.
Is anything missing now?
Truly is anything missing now?
If you thought about it, you probably could think of some things that are missing: a nightcap, a glass of beer, my kids—my kids are not here.
When we think about that question, then we can come up with all kinds of lists of what's missing.
In the human world there is missing; there are things missing.
But in Buddha's world there is nothing missing.
So for a moment when we're not thinking, there is nothing missing.
There is nothing lacking.
Rinzai has a great line about, "In your everyday activities, what do you lack right now?
This very place is the Lotus Land.
This very body is the Buddha."

This journey of ours, this practice of ours, I think, is a journey to get to know that this very body is my body and is the body of the Buddha, and to realize that not using our intellect, not just being told it, but to really feel it, to feel it with our body.
That we are both ice and we are water.
So this is Hakuin's ode to Zazen.
